summary: Protocols that use Unicode in strings such as usernames and identifiers must handle them consistently, including when comparing them. This document defines the PRECIS framework, which specifies how to prepare, enforce rules on and compare internationalized strings across application protocols.

eli5.summary: Different alphabets have many tricky look-alike letters. This sets out common rules so that two names that should match are treated as the same, and tricks are caught.

questions: how to compare unicode usernames safely
what is the difference between identifierclass and freeformclass
how to compare unicode strings safely
subtitle: A shared rulebook for checking and comparing Unicode strings such as usernames, passwords and nicknames in Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Protocols that accept Unicode text in slots such as addresses and identifiers need consistent rules, or two strings that look the same can be treated as different (or the reverse), which breaks authentication and authorization. The older Stringprep framework was tied to one Unicode version.
tldr.mechanism: PRECIS defines two string classes, IdentifierClass and FreeformClass, built from Unicode code point properties, plus a set of rules (width mapping, additional mapping, case mapping, normalization, directionality) that protocols combine into profiles, applied in a fixed order.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 7564 and gives application protocols a reusable, Unicode-version-agile way to prepare, enforce and compare strings. The RFC warns that profiles must not be multiplied beyond necessity and that confusable characters cannot be fully solved.

today: RFC 8264 is a Proposed Standard from October 2017 that obsoletes RFC 7564, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the base classes used by the username and password profiles in RFC 8265 and the nickname profile in RFC 8266.

sections.title: Why PRECIS Exists
sections.content:
Application protocols that carry Unicode code points in protocol strings need to handle them properly. That means enforcing internationalization rules for strings placed in slots such as addresses and identifiers, and comparing them correctly, for example when making authentication or authorization decisions. RFC 8264 defines the PRECIS framework (preparation, enforcement and comparison of internationalized strings) for this job, and it obsoletes RFC 7564.

Many older protocols used Stringprep (RFC 3454). Stringprep was tied to Unicode version 3.2, and the newer IDNA2008 specifications for domain names stopped using it. That pushed other users of Stringprep to look for a different approach. PRECIS is built on Unicode code point properties, so it is more agile as Unicode versions change, although the RFC says complete agility cannot be realized in practice.

PRECIS is restricted to Unicode. It does not support any other coded character set. It is also similar to IDNA2008 and reuses some of its character categories, but it adds categories for the needs of application protocols other than DNS.
sections.eli5: People type names in many alphabets, and computers can disagree about whether two names match. PRECIS is a newer, fairer set of rules so everyone agrees.

sections.title: Preparation, Enforcement and Comparison
sections.content:
The RFC separates three actions an entity can take on a string.

  • Enforcement applies all the rules of a string class or profile to one input string, to check that it conforms and can be used in a given protocol slot.
  • Comparison applies all the rules to two input strings to decide whether they are equivalent.
  • Preparation mainly ensures that the code points in a string are allowed by the string class, and sometimes applies some of the rules. It does not guarantee that the string conforms to all rules.

In most cases, authoritative entities such as servers are responsible for enforcement, while subsidiary entities such as clients only do preparation. Clients may lack the memory and processing power for steps such as Unicode normalization, and a client cannot necessarily be trusted to generate strings properly in security-sensitive contexts.

The RFC also stresses that turning an input string into an output string is rarely reversible. Case mapping turns StPeter into stpeter, and the original capitalization is lost.
sections.eli5: Checking a name is like a bouncer reading one ID. Comparing is checking whether two IDs belong to the same person. The kid at the door can do a quick look, but the head bouncer makes the final call.

sections.title: The Two String Classes
sections.content:
After analysing existing Stringprep profiles, the community concluded that most uses fit two string classes.

  • IdentifierClass is for strings that identify or address a network entity, such as a user account, a chat room, a data feed or a file. It prioritizes safety over expressiveness.
  • FreeformClass is for free-form strings, including passwords and human-friendly nicknames. It allows nearly any Unicode code point, so it prioritizes expressiveness over safety.

Each class is defined by four behavioral rules: which code points are valid, which are allowed only if a contextual rule is met, which are disallowed, and what to do with unassigned code points (they are treated as disallowed). The classes use an inclusion model: only explicitly allowed code points are permitted, and anything else is forbidden.

Both classes treat letters and digits and printable ASCII (U+0021 through U+007E) as valid, require a contextual rule for joining code points and some exceptions, and disallow old Hangul Jamo, control code points and ignorable code points. They differ on spaces, symbols, punctuation, code points with compatibility equivalents, and other letters and digits: the IdentifierClass disallows them, and the FreeformClass allows them.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of name tags. The strict one only allows plain letters and numbers so nobody gets fooled. The loose one lets you use almost any character, which is fun but riskier.

sections.title: Profiles and Their Rules
sections.content:
The classes set the baseline, and a profile adds the rest. A profile MUST define five rules: width mapping, additional mapping (if any), case mapping, normalization and directionality. It MAY restrict the allowed code points further but MUST NOT add as valid any code point the base class disallows. Profile names have the form Profilename of BaseClass, for example the OpaqueString profile of the FreeformClass.

  • Width mapping maps fullwidth and halfwidth code points to their decomposition mappings. With NFC it is generally RECOMMENDED.
  • Additional mapping covers things such as delimiters or mapping non-ASCII spaces to SPACE (U+0020).
  • Case mapping: if wanted, using the Unicode toLowerCase() operation is RECOMMENDED over toCaseFold(). For passwords, mapping to lowercase is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  • Normalization: Normalization Form C (NFC) is RECOMMENDED. NFKC and NFKD can lose information, so extreme care is needed.
  • Directionality: the framework defines no new rule. Profile authors who think they need one are advised to use the IDNA2008 Bidi Rule for IdentifierClass-based profiles or the Unicode bidirectional algorithm for FreeformClass-based ones.

The RFC admits there are already too many profiles and says they must not be multiplied beyond necessity, because many profiles mean different behavior across applications.
sections.eli5: A profile is a house rule added to the club rulebook, like whether capital letters count. Too many house rules make everyone confused, so the RFC asks people to keep them few.

sections.title: Order of Operations and Using PRECIS
sections.content:
To compare strings properly, the rules of a class or profile MUST be applied in this order: width mapping, additional mapping, case mapping, normalization, directionality, and finally the behavioral rules that decide whether each code point is valid, contextual, disallowed or unassigned.

Applying the rules is not always idempotent. For example, with NFKC, normalizing after case mapping can still yield uppercase characters for some code points. So an implementation SHOULD reapply the rules until the output is stable, and if it is not stable after three additional applications, it SHOULD stop and reject the input as invalid.

For application designers, the RFC gives guidance. Internationalization is not made easy by PRECIS, and often the safest option is to support only ASCII. Developers should not define their own profile unless absolutely necessary. They should specify which entities do preparation, enforcement and comparison, when they must do it, and which protocol slots are checked against which profiles. A protocol MAY also exclude further code points for a slot. Constructs that do not map directly to a class can be built at the application layer, such as a username made of space-separated IdentifierClass parts.
sections.eli5: Doing the steps in a different order can give a different answer, like putting on shoes before socks. So the rulebook fixes the order, and says to repeat a few times if needed.

sections.title: Code Point Properties and IANA Registries
sections.content:
To implement the classes, the RFC reviews Unicode code point properties and defines an algorithm that gives each code point a derived property value: PVALID, CONTEXTJ or CONTEXTO (contextual rule required), DISALLOWED, UNASSIGNED, or class-specific values such as ID_DIS and FREE_PVAL. The steps of the algorithm MUST NOT be reordered, because that would give inconsistent results across implementations.

The algorithm uses eighteen categories lettered A to R. The first ten (A to J) come from IDNA2008 in RFC 5892, and some of them are not used by PRECIS. The next eight (K to R) are specific to PRECIS.

  • K ASCII7: printable code points U+0021 to U+007E.
  • L Controls, such as LINE FEED (U+000A).
  • M PrecisIgnorableProperties: default-ignorable and noncharacter code points.
  • N Spaces (general category Zs), O Symbols, P Punctuation.
  • Q HasCompat: code points that change under Normalization Form KC.
  • R OtherLetterDigits: general categories Lt, Nl, No and Me.

Because the rules rely on properties rather than fixed tables, changes in Unicode that do not affect the outcome do not affect the framework.

IANA maintains three registries for PRECIS. The "PRECIS Derived Property Value" registry records the derived properties for each Unicode version starting from 6.3. The "PRECIS Base Classes" registry has the policy "RFC Required" and holds FreeformClass (Section 4.3) and IdentifierClass (Section 4.2). The "PRECIS Profiles" registry uses "Expert Review", which eases registration while making sure that applicants get guidance on subtle internationalization issues.

A profile registration gives its name, base class, applicability, the Stringprep profile it replaces, the five rules, which entities enforce them and when, and a specification pointer. Reviewers are asked, among other things, whether an existing class or profile would solve the problem, whether the profile reduces user surprise, and whether it introduces new security concerns such as false accepts.

The RFC also asks IANA not to make further updates to the derived property registry until the IESG reports that the issues about Unicode normalization described in Section 13.5 have been settled.
sections.eli5: Every character gets sorted into boxes with labels like letter, space or symbol. Which boxes are allowed depends on which name tag you are making. There is also an official notebook where every addition is written down and checked by experts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If strings that look the same to users are treated as different, or strings that look different are treated as the same, users get confused and security suffers through false accepts and false rejects (discussed in RFC 6943). The RFC encourages protocols that use PRECIS to describe the security implications of their comparison choices.

IdentifierClass strings are relatively safe, since they exclude spaces, code points with compatibility equivalents and almost all symbols and punctuation, but they can still hold confusable code points. FreeformClass strings can contain virtually any code point, so designers are encouraged to profile the IdentifierClass where feasible, or restrict a FreeformClass profile as tightly as possible.

Confusable characters are a real problem. The RFC gives examples such as CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER A (U+0430) versus LATIN SMALL LETTER A (U+0061), and even ju1iet versus juliet. PRECIS does not map look-alike characters together or ban characters because they resemble others. Services SHOULD define a policy for which scripts may be registered and SHOULD forbid strings that mix code points from more than one script. User software SHOULD define how strings are presented to users.

For passwords, it is NOT RECOMMENDED to remove whole categories such as symbols or punctuation, or to map to lowercase. Case should be preserved and compared case-sensitively. If a password is fed into a hash function, the client must prepare it first, since the server never sees the plaintext.
sections.eli5: Some letters in different alphabets look almost identical, like twins in disguise. Nobody can fully stop this, so the RFC tells website owners to limit which alphabets they accept.

sections.title: Interoperability and Unicode Changes
sections.content:
PRECIS supports only Unicode. If a system uses another coded character set, the rules cannot be applied to it, and converting from a local character set to Unicode is left to the application. The exact encoding (often UTF-8) is also a matter for the application protocol.

Unicode itself changes between versions, and that can destabilize PRECIS categories. The RFC gives examples: three code points changed their General Category between Unicode 5.2 and 6.0, the HasCompat result for a string can change when a new precomposed character is added, and the East Asian width property is not guaranteed to be stable.

The RFC also warns that handling of some code points may change. A question raised during the review of Unicode 7.0 for IDNA led to re-analysis of the normalization rules that PRECIS inherited. As written, the issues were unsettled, and the specification was likely to be updated. Possible changes include narrowing the LetterDigits category, excluding some code points, defining more additional mapping rules, and adding alternative normalization methods. The advice for avoiding trouble is to use the more restrictive IdentifierClass whenever possible, and with the FreeformClass to allow only a restricted set of code points.
sections.eli5: The list of characters keeps growing over time, so the rulebook might need small updates later. Using the strict name tag is the safest way to avoid surprises.
